title: No Banner on the Water
text:
The forty-four travelers boarded at four different harbors.

Cell Three arrived first as medical freight escorts. Cell Five joined two days later under contracts issued by a failed apothecary. Tae Muyeon boarded with the deck laborers before sunrise. Huo Wujin appeared at noon carrying a cook’s knife, three onions and the confidence of a man who had never been asked to prove he could cook.

Sera and Rhen came last.

Their papers named them as a provincial physician and his wife. The harbor clerk looked at Sera’s hands, then at the medicine cases Rhen carried.

[[speaker:captain]]“Assistant?”

[[speaker:sera]]“Accountant.”

[[speaker:rhen]]“She also corrects my diagnoses.”

[[speaker:sera]]“Frequently.”

The clerk stamped both papers to end the conversation.

Nobody assembled on deck. Mei Rulan’s group slept near the bow. Seo Dabin’s people occupied the lower cargo racks. Tae worked the central mast. Huo argued with the galley stove. Signals moved through ordinary tasks: a folded sail, a bucket placed handle-out, a complaint about onions that told Sera the harbor watch had searched the stern.

The black-salt vessel left Wuyue looking exactly as unimportant as Lu had intended. Its patched sail pulled unevenly. Its old hull complained whenever the current changed. No banner identified a clan, Domain or army.

Sera spent the first hour beside strangers who had served under her for three years. None looked at her for instruction. They watched ropes, cargo and the sailors whose habits might reveal danger.

Rhen found the separation more difficult.

At midday, Sera’s cup slid as the vessel crossed its first hard current. His hand moved from six paces away. He stopped before touching it.

A deckhand caught the cup instead.

[[speaker:customer]]“Careful, mistress.”

[[speaker:sera]]“Thank you.”

Rhen turned toward the sea with the expression of a man who had lost a medical dispute.

That evening, their covers placed them at different tables. Sera ate with medicine traders. Rhen sat between a rope merchant and Huo, who was still explaining why the stew’s failures were structural rather than culinary.

Sera lifted one eyebrow across the room.

Rhen looked away too slowly.

Mei passed behind him carrying bowls.

[[speaker:rulan]]“You do not know her.”

[[speaker:rhen]]“I am aware.”

[[speaker:rulan]]“Your face is not.”

The expedition entered the Black Current without marching, saluting or gathering once as a visible force.

Only after darkness covered the deck did Sera pass Rhen beside the water casks. Their hands touched for one step.

Neither stopped.

No banner moved above them.

The sea did not know Wuyue had crossed.

title: Medicine for a Voyage That Does Not Exist
text:
Seo Dabin rejected the first water cask before anyone drank from it.

The water was clean. The resin sealing the lid was not. Northern cold had contracted the wood and pressed preservative into the upper layer, creating a bitter compound harmless in warm ports but dangerous after prolonged circulation.

[[speaker:dabin]]“Not poison.”

A sailor sighed with relief.

[[speaker:dabin]]“That does not mean you drink it.”

She checked every cask, ration packet and cooking jar without asking Rhen to confirm her conclusions. He observed until she reached the dried kelp.

[[speaker:rhen]]“What changes below freezing?”

[[speaker:dabin]]“Texture.”

[[speaker:rhen]]“Inside the patient.”

Seo paused. The kelp’s mineral content would slow absorption in familiar climates. In northern cold, constricted circulation could keep those minerals concentrated near the stomach meridian long enough to resemble early poisoning.

She revised the ration order herself.

Rhen had taught without taking the diagnosis from her.

The lesson became real before sunset. A deckhand collapsed while hauling the lower sail. His lips had gone pale. Sweat stood on his forehead despite the cold. The captain assumed contaminated water and ordered the casks thrown overboard.

Seo stopped him.

The patient had drunk from a private flask filled at the harbor. No one else sharing his meal showed symptoms. His pulse weakened whenever the ship climbed, then recovered in the trough.

[[speaker:dabin]]“Not ingested poison. Pressure and motion.”

She found an old rib injury bound too tightly beneath his coat. Cold had stiffened the scar tissue. Each climb of the bow compressed his breathing until panic tightened the binding further.

Seo cut the cloth, changed his position and warmed the scar gradually. Rhen passed her two needles only after she named their purpose.

The sailor’s color returned.

[[speaker:captain]]“You saved our water.”

[[speaker:dabin]]“I saved your sailor. The water remains unpleasant.”

By nightfall, the crew had stopped treating the forty medical escorts as suspicious cargo. The captain offered them access to the sheltered lower deck and the vessel’s true current charts.

Sera accepted neither as a favor. She exchanged treatment, ration inspection and two shifts of skilled labor. Gratitude created stories. Fair trade created an ordinary reason to cooperate again.

Rhen found Seo rechecking the rejected cask.

[[speaker:rhen]]“You were correct.”

[[speaker:dabin]]“About which part?”

[[speaker:rhen]]“The water is unpleasant.”

She stared at him.

From the galley, Huo announced that dinner would improve it.

Seo sealed the cask.

[[speaker:dabin]]“Then we may need the contamination.”

title: Tae Recognizes the Poison
text:
Tae Muyeon found the residue beneath six inches of bilge water.

It looked like grey salt caught between two hull boards. The ship had carried black salt years earlier, and no ordinary sailor would have separated one old mineral stain from another. Tae felt it answer the metal pathways in his body.

One repaired meridian tightened.

The reaction was small. The memory was not.

A treatment frame beneath Cloudrest. His heart stopping between beats. Grey venom following the exact internal routes that made his horizon possible. Months rebuilding strength without accepting advancement from Rhen’s passive.

Tae’s hand closed around the board. Iron pressure entered the hull. For one breath, every nail from bow to stern answered him.

He could have torn the contaminated section free.

He released the pressure instead.

[[speaker:tae]]“Seo.”

He did not call Rhen.

Seo Dabin descended wearing two layers of gloves. She listened while Tae described sensation, sequence and the difference between this residue and the poison that nearly killed him. He gave evidence before anger could turn resemblance into certainty.

The compound was spent, perhaps years old. Cold moisture had preserved one metallic binder. When Seo exposed it to a thread of ordinary internal energy, nothing happened. When Tae circulated through one iron meridian, the residue aligned toward him.

[[speaker:dabin]]“Related mechanism.”

[[speaker:tae]]“Same school.”

[[speaker:dabin]]“Possibly.”

He accepted the correction.

Rhen examined the reaction only after Seo completed her record. He confirmed that the residue recognized the architecture of Tae’s internal energy, but not whether the original poisoner had ever known Tae’s identity.

[[speaker:rhen]]“It may have been designed for metal cultivators generally.”

[[speaker:tae]]“Then I was not the target.”

Sera came down the ladder.

[[speaker:sera]]“Does that disappoint you?”

[[speaker:tae]]“It clarifies the insult.”

The old Tae might have demanded a name large enough to justify what had happened to him. The man standing in the bilge asked what the residue could teach them about the captives.

It rewarded force by learning the route force used. It remained dormant around ordinary circulation. It relied upon the victim’s strongest system to carry it deeper.

Sera added the findings to Jin’s account.

[[speaker:sera]]“Duskvein does not need to overpower the first answer.”

[[speaker:tae]]“It needs the first answer to introduce the second.”

He cut the contaminated board free with a hand tool. No pressure. No display. Seo sealed it inside three separate cases.

Above them, the ship continued north.

Tae had recognized the hand that once reached his heart.

He chose to study its fingers before breaking them.

title: Huo’s Nine Answers at Sea
text:
The raiders approached beneath white trade cloth.

Their vessel carried no visible weapons until it entered grappling distance. Then the cloth dropped, six hooked lines crossed the water and a weighted harpoon struck toward the black-salt ship’s mast.

Huo Wujin was carrying onions.

He shifted the basket into his left hand and caught the harpoon with his right.

The deck did not move.

Force that should have torn through timber entered one Meridian Wheel, changed direction through a second and dispersed through the remaining circuits until only a warm current lifted Huo’s sleeve. He set the harpoon down beside his feet.

Three raiders pulled on its chain.

Nothing returned.

A second hook struck low. Huo turned one heel. Its force curved through the hull without damaging a board and emerged upward as a gust that filled the patched sail. The merchant vessel gained speed.

He did not attack.

Every new answer remained defensive. One Wheel received impact. Another redirected tension. A third took heat from a firepot and released it harmlessly into the cold air. A fourth steadied the mast without borrowing ground from the sea.

The raiders escalated because none understood why their weapons failed. Twelve men crossed the grappling lines. Huo touched each rope once. Their own momentum folded the lines around their waists and lowered them into the water without breaking bone.

Tae watched from beside the central mast.

[[speaker:tae]]“You could have ended this before the first hook landed.”

[[speaker:huo]]“Sera did not authorize an offensive field.”

[[speaker:tae]]“You noticed.”

[[speaker:huo]]“I frequently notice instructions.”

A burning jar flew toward the passenger deck.

For the first time, Huo’s expression changed. Nine internal routes aligned. The jar stopped in the air above his palm, its flame pulled inward until oil, heat and impact became separate burdens distributed through his body. He closed his hand.

The flame went out.

Every raider felt the pressure he had not released. Their knees bent on the distant deck though Huo had not touched their vessel.

Then he let the pressure rise into empty sky. Clouds opened in a straight line for miles.

No hull shattered. No raider died.

The white-clothed vessel cut its grapples and fled.

Passengers stared at Huo. He lifted the onion basket.

[[speaker:huo]]“Cargo balance.”

Nobody believed him. Nobody possessed a better explanation.

Sera passed beside him while helping reset the sail.

[[speaker:sera]]“You remained within the field.”

[[speaker:huo]]“Barely.”

[[speaker:sera]]“That still counts.”

Praise from her landed more heavily than the harpoon. Huo returned to the galley without replying.

Tae looked once at the retreating vessel.

The raiders had survived only because Huo had chosen nine answers that were not attack.

title: The Ship That Followed No Wake
text:
Lin Tao found the pursuing ship by watching birds land on empty water.

No sail stood behind them. No wake divided the Black Current. Yet three gulls repeatedly settled, rose and moved north at the speed of a vessel whose deck could not be seen.

Lin marked the pattern with a coil of rope. The nearest Wayfinders changed work positions without looking toward the birds. Within six minutes, Sera received the warning through four ordinary movements and no spoken alarm.

The hidden craft manipulated current instead of wind. Water closed behind its hull before a wake could form, and a low concealment frame bent the horizon around it. Destroying the pursuer would reveal exactly what kind of people travelled aboard the patched merchant ship.

Sera chose a less satisfying answer.

The Black Current divided ahead. The true route turned northwest beneath stone reefs. The visible channel continued east toward military patrol water.

She allowed the pursuer to discover them.

Huo complained loudly about the sail. Tae climbed the mast in full view. Mei’s people exposed one Wuyue-made medicine wrapper near the stern, then burned it badly enough that a fragment remained readable. The merchant vessel behaved like frightened foreign smugglers trying to continue east.

At dusk, Lin cut three weighted barrels loose. Each carried a sail scrap, kitchen refuse and a slow-release oil that preserved the vessel’s scent across the surface. Current drew the false debris east.

The real ship lowered its sail and entered the reefs.

Every passenger remained still while the cold undercurrent pulled them between black stone teeth. A careless pole strike would echo through the channel. A burst of internal energy would disturb water the pursuer already knew how to read.

Rhen held no field. Tae did not reinforce the hull. Huo allowed ordinary rope to bear ordinary strain.

The ship scraped once.

Nobody solved the sound with power.

Hours later, the hidden craft passed the reef mouth and followed the false wake east. Lin watched its concealed outline distort the stars as it left.

[[speaker:sera]]“How long until they learn?”

[[speaker:lintao]]“If they search the barrels, one day. If they trust the trail, three.”

[[speaker:sera]]“Plan for one.”

The Wayfinders began changing every landing assumption.

The expedition had not escaped by becoming impossible to follow.

Sera had given pursuit a more believable road than the one she took.

title: A Duskvein Needle in a Dead Sailor
text:
The pursuing craft left a body in the false channel.

Lin found it after the hidden vessel turned east. A sailor floated faceup between two barrels, tied to a plank so the current could not take him below. The placement was too careful for disposal.

Sera ordered the merchant ship to pass.

The captain refused.

[[speaker:captain]]“We do not leave our dead to birds.”

He recognized the man as a coastal pilot missing for six months. Abandoning him would preserve secrecy and violate the only rule the crew considered older than profit. Sera adjusted the plan instead of treating local loyalty as an obstacle.

The body came aboard inside a sailcloth sling. Nobody touched skin. Seo Dabin controlled the examination while Rhen watched the surrounding circulation rather than the corpse. Tae stood beyond the mast, far enough that his metal pathways could not awaken residue before she was ready.

The dead man carried no weapon. One black needle rested beneath his tongue.

It had not killed him.

A second filament ran from the needle into the muscles of his jaw. Opening the mouth pulled that filament through a sealed poison pocket. The examiner’s fingers would be punctured only after curiosity had already brought the face close.

[[speaker:dabin]]“The corpse is the delivery method.”

Rhen studied the grey line around the pocket.

[[speaker:rhen]]“Delayed by cold. In warmer air it would open faster.”

Tae approached only after Seo enclosed the jaw. The needle answered his circulation with the same faint alignment as the bilge residue.

Not proof that the pursuers were Duskvein.

Proof that somebody using Duskvein’s mechanism had travelled the southern sea lanes before them.

The pilot’s palms carried older punctures. His captors had tested compounds through him repeatedly, then used his body to test whoever honored the dead. The cruelty was efficient enough to be mistaken for patience.

Huo’s pressure changed across the deck. The mast bent one finger’s width toward him.

[[speaker:huo]]“Permission to follow?”

[[speaker:sera]]“Denied.”

His gaze remained on the eastern horizon.

[[speaker:sera]]“They left him to choose our response. We do not answer with the one they prepared.”

Huo released the mast.

Seo removed the needle without breaking its poison chamber. Rhen cleansed the pilot’s body so the crew could perform their rites safely, then stepped back. The captain wrapped the man in clean sailcloth and spoke his name where the sea could hear it.

The expedition learned three things.

Duskvein’s methods had crossed the water before them. Its traps survived after the battlefield appeared empty. And even a dead stranger could become a weapon if rescuers allowed urgency to decide the order of their hands.

They continued north after the burial.

Nobody touched the floating barrels.

title: Mei Rulan Borrows a Flag
text:
Mei Rulan acquired the Rimeford flag without stealing it.

The patched merchant vessel reached a frozen anchorage used by six Hearth Clans. Ranked banners occupied the stone piers. Unranked traders waited in ice water until a sponsor recognized their cargo. Foreigners without either could remain offshore until their supplies failed.

A Rimeford freight captain had a flag and no medicine clerk. His clerk had fled after discovering that half the manifest described grain already spoiled beneath the tarps. Reporting the fraud would cost the captain his contract. Concealing it would poison the Hearth settlement that bought the shipment.

Mei learned all of this while helping him argue over a docking rope.

[[speaker:rulan]]“Your third cart is listed twice.”

[[speaker:captain]]“You read Isgard marks?”

[[speaker:rulan]]“Bad handwriting is a universal language.”

She did not offer to become the missing clerk. She corrected the duplicated cart, identified the spoiled grain in front of witnesses and gave the captain a way to blame seawater damage rather than admit he had trusted the wrong merchant. Rimeford lost one cargo but avoided a winter illness. The captain kept enough standing to return home.

Only then did he ask what she wanted.

[[speaker:rulan]]“Four work parties entering separately. Temporary freight protection. No claim upon your Hearth.”

A ranked clan’s flag would have granted faster passage and created permanent attention. Rimeford’s split-grey pennant granted only the right to explain themselves at each toll. That limitation made it useful.

The captain registered Cell Five as ledger clerks, Cell Three as medicine assessors, Tae and Huo’s group as hired heavy labor, and Sera’s group as traveling physicians. None appeared important enough to justify one combined record.

Mei did not disguise forty foreigners as lifelong Rimeford people. She made them temporary workers whose accents, ignorance and mismatched clothing were expected.

At the first inspection, a guard asked why Rimeford needed so many healers.

[[speaker:rulan]]“Because its grain merchant needed fewer liars.”

The freight captain laughed with enough pain that the guard believed every word.

Beyond the anchorage, Rimeford’s position became clear. It held no rank on the Banner Ledger. Its flag could not open military roads or demand a winter charter. It survived by keeping ferries moving, supplying cold-grain and maintaining protection under Eirholt’s medical covenant.

Dependence was not identical to slavery. Eirholt physicians had saved Rimeford children without demanding military service. The Hearth paid medicine shares and honored treatment intervals in return. The relationship contained gratitude, pressure and real mutual need.

Mei folded the borrowed flag after the inspection.

[[speaker:rulan]]“We return this before it becomes a claim.”

Sera nodded.

They had entered Isgard beneath another community’s name.

Their first obligation was not to make that name pay for them.

title: The Southern Warplain
text:
Southern Isgard began with a toll fire.

Every traveler stopped before a stone basin burning blue-grey coal. Weapons remained sheathed. Medicine was declared before food. A person entering under one flag named the Hearth or ranked clan responsible for repairing any harm they caused.

The Rimeford captain placed three copper measures beside the fire.

One for road use.

One for winter shelter.

One for the Banner Ledger.

The Ledger was not merely a list of strong fighters. Its ranks decided which roads received soldiers, whose testimony could open a foreign campaign, how much tribute returned to smaller settlements and which banners could maintain large hunting forces beyond their own land.

Sera learned this while paying a toll, not from a court historian.

A Dravaryn supply column arrived behind them. Red-armored riders did not wait in the ordinary line. Their Rank Two seal opened the military lane, but their quartermaster still declared medicine. Even celebrated armies bowed to the treatment rules protected by Eirholt.

Ten minutes later, a Skeldran patrol crossed the snow without using any road. Its trackers marked their passage on the toll board anyway. Rank Three granted pursuit authority, not freedom from accounting.

No Duskvein banner appeared.

Its influence did.

Two soldiers carried black-glass antidote vials tied above the heart. A freight worker refused food after nicking his thumb on an imported thorn. The toll keeper recorded poison debt beside grain debt as if both belonged in the same column.

Beyond the fire spread the Southern Warplain.

It was not empty snow. Fortified Hearth settlements rose around hot springs, mines and grain basins. Clan roads ran straight between watchtowers because armies had used them for generations. Medicine posts stood at intervals marked by white cloth no declared fighter was permitted to violate.

Farther north, enormous banner poles broke the horizon. Their cloth could be seen before the walls beneath them.

Huo looked across the plain.

[[speaker:huo]]“They organize strength visibly.”

[[speaker:tae]]“So everyone knows where it will answer.”

Sera heard the difference. Huo saw a challenge. Tae saw a line. She saw a political map that people lived inside.

At the second toll, a guard struck the Rimeford flagstaff against stone. A false clan seal would have split. Mei’s borrowed pennant held because it was real, limited and freely lent.

[[speaker:captain]]“Rimeford protection ends at the north fork.”

[[speaker:sera]]“Then our debt ends there too?”

The captain studied her.

[[speaker:captain]]“Debts end when both sides agree they were paid.”

That answer explained more of Isgard than the banners.

The ranked clans governed through seals and force. The Hearths survived through memory, service and obligations nobody wrote only once.

Forty-four foreigners entered the Warplain beneath falling snow.

For the first time, Wuyue was not the world around them.

title: The First Hearth Under Snow
text:
The whiteout erased the road before Rimeford could refuse them.

Hearth law required any settlement with a lit winter tower to shelter travelers until visibility returned. It did not require trust. The forty-four were divided among storehouses, watched by local guards and forbidden from opening medicine cases inside the central hall.

Rimeford had reason to be cautious. Foreign remedies could create symptoms Eirholt physicians would later misread. If an unregistered healer harmed a patient, Eirholt could suspend the Hearth’s protection until responsibility was established. One generous decision might cost an entire winter of treatment.

Sera accepted the restriction.

Then two ferry crews began fighting over the last ice-safe crossing.

The eastern crew held the old right. The western landing had repaired the cables after spring flood and claimed that labor transferred authority. With the river freezing unevenly, only one ferry could run before morning. Both settlements had medicine waiting across the water.

A local captain demanded Sera choose which claim was lawful because she had presented herself as an accountant.

[[speaker:sera]]“I said I kept accounts.”

[[speaker:captain]]“Then count what each side loses.”

She did.

The eastern claim rested on inherited right. The western claim rested on current maintenance. Neither answered why one ferry had to carry one settlement’s cargo. The weight limit allowed both medicine loads if grain moved later. The crews refused because whichever flag crossed first would be recorded as the rightful operator for the winter.

Sera separated passage from precedent.

Both crews would load medicine together. The ferry would carry no Hearth flag, only Eirholt’s white treatment cloth. The toll record would state that emergency medical passage created no future right. After the storm, the two settlements could argue ownership without patients paying for the timing.

The captain read the wording twice.

[[speaker:captain]]“You speak like a Banner clerk.”

[[speaker:sera]]“I run a tea shop.”

[[speaker:captain]]“Is that a Wuyue office?”

[[speaker:sera]]“On difficult days.”

The ferry crossed under white cloth.

During unloading, one western worker collapsed with cold injury complicated by a black-glass stimulant. Rimeford’s physician hesitated to let foreigners touch him. Seo Dabin named the stimulant’s visible signs without opening her case. Rhen described only what delay would do. Neither demanded authority.

The local physician made the decision and invited them in.

Seo neutralized the stimulant’s remaining cycle. Rhen restored damaged tissue slowly enough that the patient’s body did not advertise impossible healing. The Rimeford physician watched every step and retained responsibility for aftercare.

By dawn, the whiteout had buried every foreign footprint outside the wall.

Rimeford offered guides to the north fork. Not soldiers. Not allegiance. Guides who knew which tolls accepted temporary work seals and which roads belonged to Duskvein suppliers.

Sera accepted and paid the same rate Rimeford paid its own.

Their first ally in Isgard was not a ranked clan.

It was a Hearth that trusted them exactly as far as their actions had earned.

title: Forty Footprints Become Four
text:
At the north fork, forty footprints became four trails.

Cell Three continued beneath Rimeford medicine papers toward the winter treatment road. Cell Five joined a freight caravan serving Ledger clerks. Tae and Huo took eight operatives through the iron-market route as hired protection. The remaining Quiet Hands divided between them according to cover, not combat preference.

Sera and Rhen travelled with the smallest group.

Their papers described an argumentative married physician pair seeking frostroot and temporary clinic work. Mei had written argumentative after observing them pack.

[[speaker:sera]]“She added that without permission.”

[[speaker:rhen]]“Accuracy may not require permission.”

[[speaker:sera]]“You packed a kettle into occupied territory.”

[[speaker:rhen]]“We have used it.”

The Rimeford guide walking ahead stopped pretending not to listen. Their cover improved with every genuine disagreement.

The four parties carried no complete rendezvous map. Each knew one meeting window and one absence response. If Cell Three failed to appear, Cell Five would not search immediately; it would place a harmless market notice that opened a second location. If two parties vanished, Sera’s group would assume compromise and abandon every shared identity.

Rhen disliked the rule that could leave wounded people unsearched for twelve hours.

He accepted it because rushing toward a missing signal was precisely how Duskvein converted care into a second captive. His medical veto applied when a patient existed within reach, not to every fear he could imagine beyond the horizon.

The first separation happened at a stone shrine buried to its roofline in snow. Mei adjusted Sera’s collar like a clerk correcting a traveler’s poor appearance.

[[speaker:rulan]]“You know each other too well.”

[[speaker:sera]]“We are married in this cover.”

[[speaker:rulan]]“Yes. Try not to look happily married. Northern traders distrust it.”

Rhen considered this.

[[speaker:rhen]]“Should we argue more?”

[[speaker:sera]]“You can carry both medicine cases.”

Mei nodded.

[[speaker:rulan]]“Perfect.”

They separated without farewell.

By dusk, no observer could have connected the medicine assessors entering an Eirholt road with the freight clerks bargaining for charcoal. Tae and Huo’s group looked too conspicuous to be covert and therefore like ordinary hired muscle. Sera’s party looked tired, cold and mildly irritated with one another.

At four different inns, one cup was placed upside down after sunset.

All four parties had arrived.

Forty Quiet Hands had crossed Isgard’s first threshold without moving as a hand.

Ahead, Duskvein’s roads began.
